history.dynasty: None (built by the people of Mapusa during Portuguese rule)
history.period: 1842–1843 CE (established); building completed in stages thereafter
history.summary: The pastel-coloured Maruti temple stands in the centre of Mapusa town and is more than 150 years old, built by the people themselves. Under Portuguese rule no Hindu temple was permitted in Mapusa. In 1842 the travelling sage Ramdasibuva came to Mapusa, took up residence in the guesthouse and conducted bhajans in praise of Lord Maruti while worshipping his picture. After the sage left, devotees quietly placed the picture in a humble fireworks shop and worshipped it in secrecy; the sage returned the next year (1843) bearing a silver idol which he gifted to the people of Mapusa. The local business community acquired the fireworks-shop land and built the temple that still stands, funded in stages. The idol faces south, believed to be the direction from which evil spirits enter, with Hanuman as the protector. The building shows 19th-century Indian temple architecture: entrances north and south, marble floors, a richly carved silver-cast doorway by local artisans, and a carved teak palanquin on the north side used in festival processions. Note: not to be confused with the Maruti Temple on Altinho Hill, Panaji — a different, better-photographed temple. No dedicated festival list was found for the Mapusa temple.

name: Maruti Temple
town_description: Mapusa is a municipal town in Bardez taluka, North Goa, about 12 km north of Panaji. It is best known for its bustling Friday market that draws vendors and shoppers from across North Goa. Though largely modern in appearance, it retains landmarks such as the Bodgeshwar temple on its outskirts and the 1840s Maruti temple in its centre.

travel.road: In the centre of Mapusa on the Anjuna–Mapusa road, about 12 km from Panaji; well connected by bus and cab
